    The Magician Of Metallurgy: Meet Rush Kane, Golf’s Latest Equipment Superstar

    Equal parts precision engineer and metallurgical sommelier, Rush Kane is filling a massive void in elite club customization - and golf’s big brands ought to be paying attention.

    By Joe Ferguson
    Published 22 hours ago In Features

    When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

    Instaread

    If you have spent any time scrolling through golf content on Instagram or TikTok recently, you may have noticed a rapidly expanding, wildly obsessive subculture: putter art.

    What can often come across as a utilitarian realm of mass-produced flatsticks has evolved into a bespoke, high-end gallery space, and amidst this exploding digital renaissance of torched finishes and custom milling, one figure is quietly separating himself from the pack.

    Meet Rush Kane - known online as "Kane Kid" - a man who is taking existing putters and forging them into bespoke masterpieces through a fascinating combination of welding, sculpting, and refinishing. He is, without hyperbole, one of the world’s most skilled metalworkers turned golf obsessives.

    Latest Videos FromGolf Monthly
    Watch full video here: Can 30-Year-Old Golf Clubs Beat Modern Tech? I Took A Retro Bag To A PGA Event

    When I sat down to interview him, I half expected the brash, loud energy typical of many of the social media personalities I speak to. Instead, I found a man who is captivatingly softly spoken and deeply considered. In an industry full of salesmen, Kane speaks with the deliberate, quiet cadence of a monk who has finally found his religion.

    I was immediately blown away by his authenticity. I have never heard anyone as totally engrossed, as relentlessly obsessed with his craft, as Rush Kane. This is a man who once locked himself away for 4 days to learn and master every nuance and facet of paintfill.

    When he talks putters, you believe every single word.

    Being a highly skilled welder is one thing - there are lots of those in the world. But to possess the architectural vision, the microscopic attention to detail, and the sheer artistry to create what Kane does? That is exceptionally rare. If you don’t believe me, just go and take a look at his Instagram page.

    His love affair with metal began at 14, when he built a custom low-rider pedal bike after becoming fascinated by something similar that featured in an MTV music video while indulging in one of his other great passions - music.

    "I just dove into metal and loved crafting with metal, and it just felt like the ultimate medium," he tells me, his eyes lighting up as he reflects on his origins. "There was just like such a divine power that you could bring out of yourself to create."

    That passion translated into a serious, highly technical career.

    For nearly 12 years, he worked for a corporation fabricating high-precision instrumentation for temperature and high-pressure calibration - systems that literally establish worldwide factory standards. In this role, Kane mastered aerospace-level TIG welding, manipulating exotic and unforgiving alloys, all while balancing this technical expertise with his love of all things art.

    From there, he pivoted to automotive performance, serving as the lead welder for Diesel Brothers on the popular Discovery Channel show for four seasons, all while teaching community welding classes in his hometown.

    But it was a single, visceral moment that altered the trajectory of his life: striking a perfectly pure five-iron while playing a round of golf with his younger brother. Kane says that single strike awakened a dormant obsession, redirecting his metallurgical genius toward the most agonizingly precise instrument in sports: the putter.

    What makes Kane a true savant is his staggering understanding of the materials themselves. Listening to him discuss the various types and grades of metal is like listening to a sommelier discuss the terroir of a grand cru Burgundy.

    He exclusively takes on projects involving high-tier raw metals - frequently Scotty Cameron putters, which generally utilize premium 303 stainless steel without synthetic coatings. He flat-out declines to work on cast 303 metals or putters with polymer inserts, passionately explaining how cast metals weld unpredictably and become brittle.

    Don't be fooled, however: he doesn’t just make putters look pretty; he reverse-engineers them for elite performance.

    Kane approaches each customization case-by-case, meticulously matching hosel geometry and balance points to a player’s physical structure, eye position, and natural stroke arc. For him, the art works hand in hand with the science.

    "It's not just a weld. It's not just metal," he explains. "It's all of the dynamics, all of those angles compounding to create a functional piece of high-performance artwork."

    His ability to articulately express this incredibly dense information makes him a marketing dream. He seamlessly breaks down complex torque profiles, hosel types, and face milling with an ease and a passion that has you hanging on every word.

    Ask him about the face of a putter, and he’ll give you a detailed masterclass: explaining how smooth faces offer direct energy transfer and precise feedback but are highly sensitive to moisture and debris, whereas milled faces dampen the feel and use channels - "like tire treads" - to displace moisture for environmental forgiveness.

    To see this philosophy realized, you only need to look at his personal "gamer" - a custom-built, left-handed (he’s actually right-handed, but that is another story of expression and creativity of its own!) GSS (German Stainless Steel) putter crafted in collaboration with local Utah maker Weston Maughan. It is a masterpiece featuring a smooth, triple-pass micromilled face, freehand engravings, and a hand-shaped, hand-torched steel neck extension that fades beautifully from blue to purple, all dialed in to a minimal 7-degree toe hang.

    It is very Rush Kane.

    Yet, for all his technical brilliance, Kane’s greatest asset might be his profound patience and lack of ego when delivering the crucial finishing touches such as paintfill. "It's really about your patience as an individual, letting the paint flow and do what it naturally does... When you try to force it, everything goes wrong," he notes.

    Alongside wrenching designs out of his own brain, Kane is equally enthusiastic about bringing other people's concepts to life.

    "I have some players that are like, 'This is my dream, and that's what I want.' And so it's really exciting for me to kind of mesh with that vision and be the engine that creates it for them."

    But Kane isn't just catering to high-end collectors - he is actively targeting a glaring structural void within elite competitive golf.

    "We have so many professionals and tour players, and if you're not in the top 15 or the top five in the world, you generally don't have access - exclusive access - to that tour department to readily deliver you and build you exactly what you need," Kane explains. "And there's a big gap in that market, and I've placed myself here to help fulfill those needs for those players that really are seeking that access."

    Currently, Kane handles all disassembly, welding, finishing, and final assembly entirely by himself, while a team manages his booming social media and order inquiries. He is even developing a "Metal Master Class" to pass on his knowledge of material recognition and metal sciences to the next generation of craftsmen.

    Looking at the landscape of golf equipment, one thing is glaringly obvious. With absolute legends of the craft like Scotty Cameron inevitably coming toward the twilight of their storied careers, massive brands need to be looking to the future.

    If I were sitting in the boardroom at Titleist, I would be breaking the bank right now to secure the services of Rush Kane as my new flagship craftsman. I don’t know if you’d get him (he seems pretty content with his work right now), but he has the pedigree, the vision, and the undeniable on-camera presence to carry the torch for the next decade.

    As for me? I’m not waiting for the corporate giants to make their move. I will be putting my hand firmly into my own pocket to commission an early Rush Kane piece. Because after spending just an hour with the man, I am absolutely convinced he is going to ‘blow up’ as the kids say.

    Securing a Kane Kid putter right now might not be just buying a golf club; it feels to me exactly like getting your hands on an early Banksy.

    Joe Ferguson

    Staff Writer

    Joe has worked in the golf industry for nearly 20 years in a variety of roles. After a successful amateur career being involved in England squads at every age group, Joe completed his PGA degree qualification in 2014 as one of the top ten graduates in his training year and subsequently went on to become Head PGA Professional at Ryder Cup venue The Celtic Manor Resort. Equipment has always been a huge passion of Joe’s, and during his time at Celtic Manor, he headed up the National Fitting Centres for both Titleist and TaylorMade.
